questiontext.text:
Match the meristematic tissues with their characteristic locations in flowering plants:

List I (Meristem)List II (Location)
(A) Root apical meristem(i) Axils of leaves
(B) Axillary bud(ii) Tip of a root
(C) Intercalary meristem(iii) Mature regions of woody axis
(D) Lateral meristem(iv) Between mature tissues in grasses

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Meristems in plants are specialised regions of active cell division classified according to their position in the plant body and the stage of development at which they appear.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
1. Root apical meristem occupies the tip of a root and produces primary root tissues.
2. Axillary buds are formed from cells left behind by the shoot apical meristem during leaf formation and stem elongation, and are present in the axils of leaves.
3. Intercalary meristem occurs between mature tissues, particularly in grasses, where it regenerates parts removed by grazing herbivores.
4. Lateral (secondary) meristems are cylindrical meristems occurring in the mature regions of roots and shoots of plants that produce a woody axis.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Matching each meristem to its exact location gives: Root apical meristem corresponds to tip of a root (A-ii); Axillary bud corresponds to axils of leaves (B-i); Intercalary meristem corresponds to between mature tissues in grasses (C-iv); Lateral meristem corresponds to mature regions of woody axis (D-iii).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-ii, B-i, C-iv, D-iii.

questiontext.text:
Match the simple permanent tissues with their characteristic structural features:

List I (Simple Tissue)List II (Characteristic Feature)
(A) Parenchyma(i) Corner thickenings of cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin
(B) Collenchyma(ii) Spherical or oval dead cells with very narrow lumen
(C) Sclerenchyma fibres(iii) Thin cellulosic walls, generally isodiametric cells
(D) Sclereids(iv) Thick-walled, elongated, and pointed dead cells

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Simple permanent tissues are composed of only one type of cell and include parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma (fibres and sclereids), each distinguished by cell shape, wall composition, and presence or absence of protoplast.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
1. Parenchyma cells are generally isodiametric with thin walls made up of cellulose.
2. Collenchyma cells are much thickened at the corners due to deposition of cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin, and lack intercellular spaces.
3. Sclerenchyma fibres are thick-walled, elongated, and pointed dead cells generally occurring in groups.
4. Sclereids are spherical, oval, or cylindrical, highly thickened dead cells with very narrow cavities (lumen), found in fruit walls of nuts and pulp of fruits like guava, pear, and sapota.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Pairing each tissue with its structural feature gives: Parenchyma – thin cellulosic walls, generally isodiametric cells (A-iii); Collenchyma – corner thickenings of cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin (B-i); Sclerenchyma fibres – thick-walled, elongated, and pointed dead cells (C-iv); Sclereids – spherical or oval dead cells with very narrow lumen (D-ii).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-iii, B-i, C-iv, D-ii.

questiontext.text:
Match the elements of complex tissues with their characteristic properties:

List I (Tissue Element)List II (Property)
(A) Tracheids(i) Absent in most monocotyledons
(B) Vessels(ii) Maintain pressure gradient in sieve tubes
(C) Companion cells(iii) Characteristic feature of angiosperms, absent in gymnosperms
(D) Phloem parenchyma(iv) Elongated tube-like dead cells with tapering ends

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Xylem and phloem are complex permanent tissues composed of multiple cell types working together as a functional unit for water/mineral conduction and food transport, respectively.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
1. Tracheids are elongated or tube-like dead cells with thick, lignified walls and tapering ends, found in both gymnosperms and angiosperms.
2. Vessels are long cylindrical tube-like structures made of vessel members; their presence is a characteristic feature of angiosperms, whereas gymnosperms lack vessels.
3. Companion cells are specialised parenchymatous cells closely associated with sieve tube elements that help maintain the pressure gradient in sieve tubes.
4. Phloem parenchyma consists of elongated cylindrical cells storing food and substances like resins, latex, and mucilage, and is absent in most monocotyledons.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Matching each element to its property yields: Tracheids – elongated tube-like dead cells with tapering ends (A-iv); Vessels – characteristic feature of angiosperms, absent in gymnosperms (B-iii); Companion cells – maintain pressure gradient in sieve tubes (C-ii); Phloem parenchyma – absent in most monocotyledons (D-i).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-iv, B-iii, C-ii, D-i.

questiontext.text:
Match the plant tissue structures with their descriptions:

List I (Structure)List II (Description)
(A) Cuticle(i) Usually multicellular shoot hairs preventing water loss
(B) Guard cells in grasses(ii) Thin-walled chloroplast-containing ground tissue in leaves
(C) Trichomes(iii) Waxy thick layer covering epidermis, absent in roots
(D) Mesophyll(iv) Dumb-bell shaped cells enclosing stomatal pore

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The epidermal tissue system forms the outermost covering of the plant body, while the ground tissue system comprises all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
1. Cuticle is a waxy thick layer covering the outside of the epidermis that prevents water loss, and it is absent in roots.
2. In grasses, the guard cells enclosing the stomatal pore are dumb-bell shaped (unlike the bean-shaped guard cells of dicots).
3. Trichomes are epidermal hairs on the stem; in the shoot system they are usually multicellular and help prevent water loss due to transpiration.
4. Mesophyll is the ground tissue in leaves consisting of thin-walled chloroplast-containing cells.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Matching each structure with its description gives: Cuticle – waxy thick layer covering epidermis, absent in roots (A-iii); Guard cells in grasses – dumb-bell shaped cells enclosing stomatal pore (B-iv); Trichomes – usually multicellular shoot hairs preventing water loss (C-i); Mesophyll – thin-walled chloroplast-containing ground tissue in leaves (D-ii).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-iii, B-iv, C-i, D-ii.

questiontext.text:
Match the types of vascular bundles and xylem arrangements with their defining features:

List I (Vascular Feature)List II (Characteristic)
(A) Radial vascular bundle(i) Xylem and phloem on alternate radii, as in roots
(B) Conjoint open bundle(ii) Cambium present between phloem and xylem, as in dicot stems
(C) Conjoint closed bundle(iii) Cambium absent, as in monocot stems
(D) Endarch primary xylem(iv) Protoxylem towards centre and metaxylem towards periphery

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Vascular bundles are classified based on the relative positions of xylem and phloem, the presence or absence of cambium, and the radial orientation of protoxylem and metaxylem.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
1. In radial vascular bundles, xylem and phloem are arranged in an alternate manner along different radii, as seen in roots.
2. In conjoint open vascular bundles, xylem and phloem lie along the same radius with cambium present between them, allowing secondary growth as in dicotyledonous stems.
3. In conjoint closed vascular bundles, cambium is absent between xylem and phloem, so secondary tissues are not formed, as in monocotyledons.
4. Endarch primary xylem has protoxylem lying towards the centre (pith) and metaxylem towards the periphery, as seen in stems.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Each item matches directly with its corresponding characteristic: Radial vascular bundle (A-i), Conjoint open bundle (B-ii), Conjoint closed bundle (C-iii), and Endarch primary xylem (D-iv).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-i, B-ii, C-iii, D-iv.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MATCH_Q06 - Anatomical features of roots and stems

questiontext.text:
Match the anatomical features with the plant organs in which they are characteristically observed:

List I (Anatomical Feature)List II (Plant Organ)
(A) Casparian strips(i) Dicotyledonous stem endodermis
(B) Polyarch xylem bundles(ii) Monocotyledonous stem vascular bundles
(C) Starch sheath(iii) Root endodermis
(D) Water-containing cavities(iv) Monocotyledonous root

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous roots and stems show distinct anatomical differences in their endodermis, vascular bundle number, and internal cavities.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
1. Casparian strips are waxy, water-impermeable suberin depositions on the tangential and radial walls of the root endodermis.
2. Polyarch condition (usually more than six xylem bundles) is a characteristic feature of the monocotyledonous root.
3. In a dicotyledonous stem, the cells of the endodermis are rich in starch grains, so the layer is referred to as the starch sheath.
4. In a monocotyledonous stem, phloem parenchyma is absent and water-containing cavities are present within the vascular bundles.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Matching each feature with its organ gives: Casparian strips – root endodermis (A-iii); Polyarch xylem bundles – monocotyledonous root (B-iv); Starch sheath – dicotyledonous stem endodermis (C-i); Water-containing cavities – monocotyledonous stem vascular bundles (D-ii).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-iii, B-iv, C-i, D-ii.

questiontext.text:
Match the leaf anatomical structures with their characteristic features:

List I (Leaf Structure)List II (Characteristic Feature)
(A) Palisade parenchyma(i) Large, empty, colourless adaxial cells in grass leaves
(B) Spongy parenchyma(ii) Mesophyll not differentiated into palisade and spongy layers
(C) Bulliform cells(iii) Adaxially placed elongated cells arranged vertically
(D) Isobilateral leaf mesophyll(iv) Oval or round loosely arranged cells with large air cavities

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dorsiventral (dicot) leaves and isobilateral (monocot) leaves differ in mesophyll differentiation and specialised epidermal modifications.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
1. In a dorsiventral leaf, palisade parenchyma is adaxially placed and consists of elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel to each other.
2. Spongy parenchyma is situated below the palisade cells, extending to the lower epidermis, and consists of oval or round, loosely arranged cells with numerous large spaces and air cavities.
3. In grasses, certain adaxial epidermal cells along the veins modify into large, empty, colourless bulliform cells that regulate leaf curling.
4. In an isobilateral (monocotyledonous) leaf, the mesophyll is not differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Matching each structure with its feature gives: Palisade parenchyma – adaxially placed elongated cells arranged vertically (A-iii); Spongy parenchyma – oval or round loosely arranged cells with large air cavities (B-iv); Bulliform cells – large, empty, colourless adaxial cells in grass leaves (C-i); Isobilateral leaf mesophyll – mesophyll not differentiated into palisade and spongy layers (D-ii).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-iii, B-iv, C-i, D-ii.

questiontext.text:
Match the types of wood formed during secondary growth with their characteristic features:

List I (Wood Type)List II (Characteristic Feature)
(A) Spring wood(i) Darker, higher density, narrow vessels
(B) Autumn wood(ii) Peripheral, lighter in colour, conducts water
(C) Heartwood(iii) Lighter in colour, lower density, wider vessels
(D) Sapwood(iv) Central, dark brown, dead elements, mechanical support

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Secondary xylem (wood) exhibits seasonal variations in temperate regions (spring wood and autumn wood) as well as functional differentiation in old trees (heartwood and sapwood).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
1. Spring wood (early wood) is formed when cambium is very active in spring; it has vessels with wider cavities, is lighter in colour, and has lower density.
2. Autumn wood (late wood) is formed when cambium is less active in winter; it has narrow vessels, is darker in colour, and has higher density.
3. Heartwood is the central or innermost dark brown region of secondary xylem containing deposits like tannins and resins; it comprises dead elements, does not conduct water, and provides mechanical support.
4. Sapwood is the peripheral region of secondary xylem, lighter in colour, and involved in the conduction of water and minerals from root to leaf.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Matching each wood type to its feature gives: Spring wood – lighter in colour, lower density, wider vessels (A-iii); Autumn wood – darker, higher density, narrow vessels (B-i); Heartwood – central, dark brown, dead elements, mechanical support (C-iv); Sapwood – peripheral, lighter in colour, conducts water (D-ii).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-iii, B-i, C-iv, D-ii.

questiontext.text:
Match the components associated with cork cambium activity and periderm with their respective roles or features:

List I (Component)List II (Feature / Role)
(A) Phellogen(i) Lens-shaped openings permitting gaseous exchange
(B) Phellem(ii) Parenchymatous secondary cortex formed on inner side
(C) Phelloderm(iii) Meristematic cork cambium with rectangular cells
(D) Lenticels(iv) Cork cells impervious to water due to suberin

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
As secondary growth increases stem girth, cork cambium (phellogen) develops in the cortex to replace broken outer layers, producing phellem, phelloderm, and lenticels.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
1. Phellogen (cork cambium) is a meristematic tissue made of narrow, thin-walled, nearly rectangular cells.
2. Phellem (cork) differentiates from the outer cells cut off by phellogen and is impervious to water due to suberin deposition in the cell wall.
3. Phelloderm (secondary cortex) differentiates from the inner cells cut off by phellogen and consists of parenchymatous cells.
4. Lenticels are lens-shaped openings formed when phellogen cuts off closely arranged parenchymatous cells that rupture the epidermis, permitting gaseous exchange in woody trees.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Matching each component with its feature gives: Phellogen – meristematic cork cambium with rectangular cells (A-iii); Phellem – cork cells impervious to water due to suberin (B-iv); Phelloderm – parenchymatous secondary cortex formed on inner side (C-ii); Lenticels – lens-shaped openings permitting gaseous exchange (D-i).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-iii, B-iv, C-ii, D-i.
